extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers and practitioners interested in natural science, physiology, and vision (readers of Popular Science Monthly)
extracted.subtask_description: Methods and interpretive frameworks for detecting and characterizing color-vision defects in individuals, including practical tests (Holmgren method, spectra matching, contrast tests) and theoretical interpretations (Young-Helmholtz and Hering theories).

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern sword design principles
rubrics_metrics.description: The modern sword 'combines within itself all the powers of which the weapon is capable, is good as a guard for thrusting and for cutting.' It should be 'slightly curved, but not so much as to impede its pointing power, nor so wide as to be too heavy, stiffened by grooves so as to be capable of use as a rapier; its blade, with an edge on one side along its length, is flattened at the point, where it is ribbed, for strength, into a two-edged sword. The hilt has a wider guard, and is intermediate between the rapier type and that of the basket form.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design balance: maintain pointing (thrusting) ability and cutting capacity; avoid excessive width/weight; use grooves for stiffness/lightness; pointed/ribbed termination for strength; hilt guard intermediate between rapier and basket to protect fingers while allowing thrusting and cutting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eastern (Asiatic) sword characteristics and suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Eastern races 'have almost without exception preferred a curved sword' because, given physical peculiarities and lighter armor, they administer cutting blows rather than straight downward strokes. 'The hilt of the Eastern sword is small, and the boss, or pommel, at the end of the hilt is large, so as to prevent the sword from slipping when the drawing cut is made.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curvature and hilt form are functional: curved blades favor cutting strokes; small hilt and large pommel help control the weapon during drawing cuts; ornamentation may reflect original methods of blade attachment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer comparative (matching) methods over color naming
rubrics_metrics.description: In making an examination for the diagnosis of color-blindness, nomenclature, or the naming of the colors which are presented to the person to be examined, is entirely discarded. The method of comparison is therefore the only one which should be adopted in making examinations for color-blindness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: individuals may correctly name colors yet fail matching tasks, or vice versa; use matching tasks to reveal perceptual confusions rather than language/terminology knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holmgren wool-skein matching test (practical diagnostic method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Holmgren's method consists in placing on a table before the examinee a large assortment of skeins of colored worsteds. A 'sample' skein of light-green is laid to one side, and the individual is told to select from the pile all the skeins which are of the same color — lighter or darker. If he places by the sample a shade of any other color but green, he is color-blind. To fix the particular color lacking, a purple or rose-colored skein is then used as a sample and the confusions are observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical notes: the initial light-green sample detects color-blindness generally; subsequent samples (purple/rose) help classify type (red-blind if purple matched with blue/violet; green-blind if purple matched with greens/grays). The test does not rely on naming and is simple and convenient, but may not precisely fix all types without follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solar spectrum matching method
rubrics_metrics.description: Use two solar spectra, one above the other, the upper of which is movable. A colored band is isolated in the fixed spectrum, and the upper spectrum is moved until what is supposed to be the same color is immediately above it. Or, the isolated band may be matched with a skein of colored wool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This comparative spectral matching detects perceptual shifts or shortening of the spectrum and patterns of confusion; it reproduces similar errors to the wool-skein test and helps localize spectral regions of confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast-color (shadow/ground) tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Tests based on contrast colors: when a white surface is simultaneously illuminated by a red and a white light, an object held midway casts two shadows — one cast by white light will appear red to a normal observer, the other (cast by red light) will appear green. A color-blind person will show no such difference. Similarly, rings cut from black or gray paper laid upon red or green paper and covered with tissue-paper will show differing tints to the normal viewer but not to the color-blind. Letters cut from black or gray paper on colored grounds become indistinguishable to the color-blind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These tests exploit simultaneous contrast to reveal inability to perceive opponent differences; they are useful alternatives to direct matching and can reveal functional loss for particular colors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters-on-colored-grounds test
rubrics_metrics.description: Make letters of certain colors on different colored grounds — shades of red letters, for instance, on a green ground. When these are of the requisite tints, the color-blind person is not able to distinguish them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a simple applied test closely related to real-world tasks (e.g., signage) and can detect confusion in discriminating colored symbols against colored backgrounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple methods and expectation of variation
rubrics_metrics.description: There are other methods, but they are all modifications to a greater or less extent of the foregoing, and any one who is color-blind to any considerable degree can be detected by any one, or at least by any two, of the methods indicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical diagnostic strategy: use at least two complementary tests to confirm color-vision defects; be aware of wide inter-individual variation and that no single test is universally definitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Young-Helmholtz (three-fiber) interpretive framework
rubrics_metrics.description: The Young-Helmholtz theory demands three primary or fundamental colors (red, green, violet) and corresponding retinal fibers; color-blindness arises when one or more of these fibers are lacking or functionally inactive, producing red-, green-, violet-, or total color-blindness. The theory implies particular spectral and matching behaviors (e.g., missing fiber does not make saturated primary appear black; matching confusions depend on which fiber is lacking).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this theory to predict expected percepts and spectral changes in certain defects, but note the documented evidences against it listed in the article (e.g., unexpected brightest place in shortened spectra, inability to explain extreme spectrum shortening, inconsistent neutral gray bands), so interpret test results cautiously and consider alternative frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hering opponent-process interpretive framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Hering's theory posits four fundamental colors (red, green, yellow, blue) arising from antagonistic color-substances (black-white, red-green, blue-yellow) with assimilation (A) and dissimilation (D) actions; color-blindness arises as achromatopsia (both color substances lacking) or dichromatopsia (one lacking), leading to specific patterns such as red-green blindness = blue-yellow vision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This framework explains certain phenomena (e.g., sharp demarcation in spectra) differently from Young-Helmholtz, but has objections (e.g., questions about which colors are truly antagonistic, complementary color relationships, nature of white). Use it as an alternative interpretive model and compare predicted confusions against observed test results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider retinal, optic nerve, and cerebral loci (differential diagnosis)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three distinct agents at work in the perception of color: the impression made on the retina, conduction by the optic nerve, and conversion into sensation by the cerebral center. Any one of these becoming incapacitated may produce perversion or absence of sensation. Some color-blindness cases are retinal or optic-nerve based; toxic actions (e.g., alcoholic poisoning) can produce cerebral forms. The author believes many congenital cases may be cerebral (central) in character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnostic implication: consider location of lesion (retinal vs nerve vs cerebral); include history (toxic exposures, development/use of color discrimination) and note sex/developmental patterns (women less often affected). Recognize that similar outward confusions may have different underlying loci, affecting prognosis and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations: lack of fixed laws and need for individualized interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: From study of color-blind persons it is evident that we have not yet arrived at any fixed laws governing the phenomena; all cases cannot be classed strictly as red, green, or violet blindness. Neither of the two leading hypotheses fills the demands of an acceptable theory, and there are infinite variations in mistakes among color-blind individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: avoid rigid classification; expect wide variation; do not over-interpret a single test; integrate multiple methods and clinical context; accept diagnostic uncertainty and describe observed functional deficits rather than forcing discrete categories.
